answer.summary: The manuscript reports a cross-sectional comparison of 284 self-identified ASMR participants (recruited from an ASMR Reddit forum) with 279 Qualtrics control participants who did not report ASMR. ASMR participants scored higher on the MAAS and on the Curiosity subscale of the TMS. Within the ASMR group, Curiosity correlated with average tingle intensity, and a sex difference in Curiosity was reported. The authors conclude that ASMR and mindfulness are related constructs, that ASMR may be a cognitively active process, and that mindfulness training could enhance ASMR. The group difference is plausible and modest in size. However, the design is correlational with non-equivalent recruitment, personality confounds are not addressed, the Decentering subscale was dropped after reliability problems, several reported degrees of freedom and sample sizes conflict, and the Discussion goes beyond what the data can support.

issues.claim: The group difference in mindfulness is attributed to ASMR, but the two groups were recruited and screened differently and the authors' own prior openness finding was not controlled for.

evidence.exact_quote: Recruitment of participants with ASMR was conducted via an advertisement for the study
individuals with ASMR have higher levels of the openness-to-experience personality trait

evidence.observation: Lines 115-118 list the Big Five Inventory as part of the survey. Its scores are never entered as covariates in any analysis reported on pp. 9-13, although the authors cite openness as correlated with ASMR.

issues.reasoning: ASMR participants were self-selected from an ASMR forum, while controls came from a commercial panel and were screened by watching videos. The ASMR group was not screened by video, and the ASMR group's self-report was not verified. The sex composition is also not identical as claimed: 135 of 284 ASMR participants were male (47.5%) and 123 of 279 controls were male (44.1%). Because openness, which the authors report is higher in ASMR, is closely tied to curiosity and mindful attention, the group effects on MAAS and Curiosity could partly reflect personality and recruitment differences. This weakens the central conclusion that ASMR and mindfulness are related. Covariate-adjusted analyses using the collected BFI data would be needed to address this.

issues.claim: Reported degrees of freedom and sample sizes are internally inconsistent across the text and Table 2, so the reported correlations and simple-effect tests cannot be verified.

evidence.location_hint: MAAS and TMS Curiosity correlation, lines 243-244 (p. 10)

evidence.exact_quote: was based on the total sample of ASMR participants (N = 284)
evidence.location_hint: ASMR Checklist and Mindfulness Measures, lines 264-265 (p. 11)
Simple effects of gender within ASMR group, lines 233-234 (p. 10)

evidence.observation: The Table 2 footnote states 'N = 173 ASMR participants with scores for all checklist items, MAAS items, and TMS - C items', and all correlations in the table, including MTotal with MAAS (.112) and TMS-C (.160), appear under this footnote. The text, however, reports the MTotal correlations with df = 284 and the MAAS-TMS-C correlation with df = 563.

issues.reasoning: A correlation between two measures from at most 284 ASMR participants (the whole sample is 563 including controls, but the MAAS-Curiosity correlation was computed only in the ASMR group) cannot have df = 563. The MTotal correlations are described as using N = 284 in the text but N = 173 in Table 2. The simple-effects test for sex within the ASMR group reports F(1,559), which implies the error term from the full 563-person model, not the 284-person ASMR subsample. Because the sex-difference conclusion in the Conclusions rests on this test, the inconsistency directly affects that claim. The authors should state the exact n for each analysis and recompute the tests.

issues.claim: The Decentering subscale was dropped after reliability and factor-structure problems, and the Curiosity subscale, which is the basis of most conclusions, was retained despite showing the same kind of item cross-loading.

evidence.exact_quote: Due to these heterogeneous results from our factor analyses, only the Curiosity subscale
all Curiosity subscale items and one Decentering item
The instructions to this questionnaire were slightly modified to be suitable for individuals with ASMR experiences.

evidence.observation: Lines 224-226 say all Curiosity items loaded onto the primary factor 'for both the ASMR and control participants'. Lines 219-220 on the same page state that two Decentering items also loaded onto the control group's first factor with the Curiosity items. The retained subscale is therefore not clean in either group.

issues.reasoning: The authors state that the TMS factor structure was heterogeneous and then selectively report only the subscale that appeared more stable. The Curiosity subscale is also not cleanly separated from Decentering in either group, so the selection does not establish that Curiosity is a valid, distinct construct. The instructions were modified without the modification being reported, so it is unclear whether the scale measures the same construct in both groups. Together these issues weaken confidence that the Curiosity result reflects the intended construct. The authors should report the modified instructions in full and test measurement invariance or justify the Curiosity-only analysis as exploratory.

issues.claim: The Discussion and Conclusions claim support for causal and mechanistic propositions (mindfulness training enhancing ASMR; sex-specific attentional versus cognitive mechanisms) that the correlational data cannot test.

evidence.exact_quote: The current study strongly supports the hypothesis that ASMR is related to mindfulness.

issues.reasoning: The study measured only self-reported state and trait mindfulness at one time point, with no training, no manipulation, and no measure of attentional or cognitive processing. Statements that data 'strongly support' a relation, that they 'suggest' training would enhance ASMR, and that males and females use different mechanisms go beyond the evidence. The sex difference is also based on a single interaction with p = .017 and the questionable df noted above. These claims should be reframed as hypotheses for future work, and the strength of the wording should match a cross-sectional study with group non-equivalence.

issues.claim: Several correlations are described as meaningful, including a marginal MTotal-MAAS association and a 'primarily due to' decomposition, without correction for the many tests run and without acknowledging overlap between MTotal and its component factors.

evidence.exact_quote: although this result was only marginally significant

evidence.observation: Table 2 shows MTotal correlated with Watching (.613**), Touching (.593**), Repetitive Sounds (.344**), Simulations (.289**) and Mouth Sounds (.254**). MTotal is the average of the 14 items that make up these factors, so these correlations are part-whole and not independent evidence. The table has about 30 correlations, none corrected for multiplicity.

issues.reasoning: MTotal is defined from the same items as the five factor scores, so its correlations with those factors are inflated by construction and cannot be read as separate effects. The text nonetheless attributes the TMS-Curiosity effect to the Touching and Repetitive Sounds factors (lines 271-272) and the marginal MAAS effect to Simulations (lines 275-276), each with p values near .04 to .008. With roughly 30 uncorrected tests, these isolated findings are fragile. This affects the claims about which triggers relate to curiosity and the interpretation of the cognitive-process account in the Discussion.

answer.overall_assessment: The study addresses a reasonable question and reports its main group comparison with clear effect sizes. However, the central claim rests on a non-equivalent control group, with recruitment, screening and sex composition that differ from what is described, and with a known personality correlate (openness) that was measured but not controlled. Several reported degrees of freedom and sample sizes conflict across the text and Table 2, and the reliability problems with the Decentering subscale led to selective reporting of the Curiosity subscale. The Discussion and Conclusions make causal and mechanistic claims that the cross-sectional design cannot support. The paper would benefit from covariate-adjusted analyses, a full account of screening and attrition, corrected statistics, and substantially more cautious interpretation. The evaluation is limited to the supplied material; external data and code mentioned by the authors were not available.
